title: heterogeneous-request-length-batch-splitting-sandbox
content:
TL;DR:
We ran a set of sandbox experiments that split mixed-length requests inside the continuous batcher so that kernel workloads are more homogeneous. For a mixed production-like traffic shape (40% short prompts, 40% medium, 20% long generations) we saw Q99 latency improve from ~820ms to ~420ms for latency-sensitive class while overall throughput stayed within 3% of baseline. Cost delta is small (~+2-4% GPU utilization due to extra kernel dispatches) and fairness across tenants was preserved by applying a lightweight weighted-slicing policy.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Continuous batching is performant for homogeneous token lengths but suffers when long-generation requests (e.g., >512 tokens) co-mix with short (<64 tokens) requests.
- When a batch contains a few long-running sequences the entire batch is held back by kernel and KV-cache prefill work, creating tail latency for short requests (observed in prod traces).
- Existing mitigations (tight timeouts or very small max_batch_size) cost throughput or increase per-token overhead. Need a middle ground: split mixed batches into sub-batches that improve tail without harming throughput.

Hypothesis:
- If we identify high-variance batches at enqueue time (based on estimated remaining generation length + num_input_tokens) and split them into two sub-batches — "short/fast" and "long/slow" — we can reduce latency for the short cohort while keeping GPU occupancy high for the long cohort.
- Weighted-slicing (proportional to tenant weight) ensures fairness and prevents starvation.

Experiment design:
- Implement a batch-splitting shim in the batcher: when a batch reaches capacity or timeout, compute conditional variance of predicted per-request kernel time (simple model: alpha * (input_tokens + predicted_output_tokens)). If variance > threshold, perform split.
- Split policy options tested:
  * static-split: split at median predicted time
  * percentile-split: move top 30% predicted-time to long-sub-batch
  * weighted-slice: ensure sub-batches preserve tenant weight ratios within 5%
- Also test with/without deferred-flush: let short-sub-batch flush immediately while long-sub-batch gets a small extra fill window (10ms) to improve packing.

Workloads and traffic shapes:
- Synthetic mixed traffic (seeded): 40% short (<=64 tokens), 40% medium (65-256), 20% long (257-1024). Request sizes sampled from production histogram (RUNTIME-HIST-2025-10).
- Multi-tenant scenario: 3 tenants with weights [0.6, 0.3, 0.1]. Short requests concentrated in tenant A to stress fairness.
- Baseline: Continuous-batcher default (max_batch=64, timeout=8ms, no split).

Metrics collected:
- Latency percentiles per cohort (short/medium/long): P50, P95, P99, P99.9
- Throughput (tokens/s) and tokens/GPU-second (proxy cost)
- Kernel-level breakdown from microtrace sampling: prefill, attention/kernel, kv-cache apply, memory copy
- Batch composition stats: avg sub-batch size, split-rate (% of batches split), eviction/retry events
- Fairness: deviation from tenant weight in served tokens over 5 minute windows

Implementation details (notes to self):
- Shim implemented in batcher/packaging layer (rust). New module: batch_splitter.rs with interface SplittingStrategy { decide(&Batch) -> Option<(Batch,Batch)> }
- Predictive-time heuristic: 0.9 * (input_tokens + predicted_output_tokens) + 0.1 * recent_latency_tail_estimate per client. Quick, no model training required.
- Microtrace sampling: reservoir sample 1% of requests; capture timestamps for: enqueue, batch_form, kernel_start, prefill_end, kernel_end, response_sent. Aggregate offline with trace-processor v2.
- Safety: fallback to no-split if batch contains >80% cache-miss heavy (cold KV) requests to avoid thrashing the KV-cache prefetch pattern.

Key results (runs 2025-11-04 to 2025-11-06):
- static-split (median): short cohort Q99 = 430ms (baseline 810ms), Q95 = 72ms (baseline 120ms). Long cohort Q99 increased from 900ms to 1020ms. Overall tokens/s -1.8%. Split-rate ~22%.
- percentile-split (top30 move): short cohort Q99 = 410ms, long cohort Q99 = 1060ms, tokens/s -2.9%. Best tail improvement but higher cost due to smaller long-batch packing efficiency.
- weighted-slice + deferred-flush (10ms): short cohort Q99 = 420ms, long cohort Q99 = 980ms, tokens/s -1.2%, fairness deviation <3%. Split-rate ~18%.
- Microtrace breakdown (short cohort, percentile-split): prefill reduced by ~45% per-request, kernel busy time per short request reduced by ~38%.
- GPU utilization: +2.6% average because more kernel invocations (smaller batches) but more uniform compute per call; cost per token change estimated +3%.

Observations from microtraces and profiler (nvprof samples):
- When short and long share a kernel call we see larger variance in kernel occupancy; small requests pay overhead for workspace allocation and kv-cache prefill that could have been amortized if packed with similar-length requests.
- Deferred-flush window (7-12ms) helps long-sub-batches recover packing without materially impacting short latency if weighted-slice prevents domination.
- Cold KV-cache requests dominate worst tails; splitting helps only if long requests are not also cold-cache heavy. We need separate cold-cache detection upstream (fast flag) to avoid bad splits.

Risks / tradeoffs:
- Increased number of kernel launches increases driver overhead and slightly higher GPU consumption.
- More complex decision logic increases scheduler CPU cost and complexity for correctness (race conditions with preemption).
- Potential for tenant unfairness if weighted guarantees are not tight; must add metric-level SLAs before rollout.

Next steps / action items:
- (Priya) Harden batch_splitter.rs with unit tests and thread-safety checks (due 2025-11-12).
- (Ethan) Add cold-kv detection flag to front of batcher pipeline and re-run percentiles (due 2025-11-10).
- (María) Run longer 24h soak with traffic replay for tokens/second stability and tenant fairness (start 2025-11-09).
- (Liam) Add experiment in dedicated cluster with quantized model to quantify cost delta on a 4xA100 config.
- Draft a short runbook for ops: when to enable split/disable on overload, how to interpret fairness breach alerts.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should the split decision be reactive (based on current queue) or proactive (use short-term arrival forecast)? Which is more stable under bursty arrivals?
- Can we reduce kernel launch overhead via batched multi-stream dispatch (combine many small kernels into a single launch)? Hardware tradeoffs unknown.
- What are SLO guardrails for long-cohort inflation — acceptable P99 increase? Product needs input.

Appendix: quick commands and artifacts
- Trace processor: trace-processor --input traces/run-2025-11-05-reservoir.json --group-by cohort --output analysis/hetero-split-2025-11-05.csv
- GitHub PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2345 (branch: feature/hetero-split)
- JIRA: RUNTIME-1023 (epic: batcher-splits)
- Quick plot: short_vs_baseline_q99.png (attached in drive folder)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a sandbox doc; suggestions welcome. Priority is reducing short-request tail without blowing up tokens/GPU cost. If product is okay with small P99 inflation for long cohort we can enable adaptive-percentile split behind a feature flag for internal beta.
